slides.title: Classifying Kidney Transplant Rejection from Biopsy RNA
paragraphs: This project asks a specific question: once a kidney transplant biopsy has been collected, can its RNA measurements classify the rejection diagnosis recorded for that tissue? I will explain the measurements, compare four models, and show the prediction software.
actions: State the research question, then introduce transplant rejection.
visible_cues: Classifying Kidney Transplant Rejection from Biopsy RNA

slides.title: Transplant rejection and kidney biopsy: key concepts
paragraphs: A kidney transplant gives a person a donor kidney. The recipient's immune system can recognize it as foreign and attack it. That immune response is rejection.

A biopsy is a small tissue sample. It can supply two kinds of evidence. A specialist examines thin sections under a microscope for injury and inflammation. Histology means studying tissue this way. The other branch is molecular measurement, which gives us the RNA counts used by the model.

In this dataset, the recorded diagnoses come from histological assessment, rescored using Banff 2019 criteria. Those diagnoses provide the answers used to train and evaluate the classifier. The molecular measurements provide its inputs.
Why seek another assessment when the tissue has already been examined? That is the reason for the proposed use on the next slide.
actions: Follow the two branches from biopsy tissue to the recorded diagnosis and the model inputs.
visible_cues: Rejection: the recipient's immune system attacks the donated kidney.
Two kinds of evidence from tissue already collected
Biopsy tissue: a small sample from the kidney
Microscopic examination (histology): recorded diagnosis
Molecular measurements: inputs to the model

slides.title: Possible Use: Molecular Second Opinion for Ambiguous Biopsies
paragraphs: The possible use is a molecular second opinion for ambiguous biopsies. Sometimes the microscopic findings are borderline or conflict with other clinical evidence. A specialist then needs to weigh the available information.

Histology shows tissue appearance. RNA messages provide information about gene activity in that tissue. Because they describe different things, a molecular assessment could add useful evidence for specialist review.

This project tests how well RNA measurements classify recorded diagnoses and builds software that can score further specimens. It does not directly test whether the score helps resolve an ambiguous biopsy. The useful next comparison is whether adding the score improves assessment in those difficult cases.
actions: Connect the two kinds of evidence to specialist review, then state what this project tests.
visible_cues: Sometimes the microscopic findings are borderline or conflict with other clinical evidence.

RNA measurements: gene activity

slides.title: Evidence for a molecular second opinion
paragraphs: There is a clinical research basis for this proposal. Banff guidance supports the classification of transplant biopsy findings and considers validated molecular tests in selected difficult cases.

Rosales and colleagues used B-HOT, the same panel of RNA measurements used here. Patients who later developed chronic active antibody-mediated rejection had higher initial rejection-related molecular scores as a group, despite lacking that diagnosis on the initial biopsy. Antibody-mediated rejection is a form involving immune proteins called antibodies.

That study supports investigating information beyond the initial tissue diagnosis. Its later-outcome finding belongs to that external study. This project classifies recorded diagnoses. Added value in ambiguous cases remains untested.
actions: Explain the two evidence rows, then connect them to the project question.

slides.title: Recorded diagnoses
paragraphs: The study records four diagnoses. Antibody-mediated rejection involves antibodies, proteins made by the immune system. T-cell-mediated rejection involves T cells, a type of immune cell. Mixed rejection includes both processes.
Those three diagnoses all count as rejection in this project. The fourth category, no rejection, supplies the comparison group. This produces the two-category question the model will answer.
We also retain the original diagnoses. That will let us see whether the missed cases are concentrated in a particular kind of rejection.
actions: Read down the diagnosis table and show how the three rejection diagnoses share one label.
visible_cues: Recorded diagnosis / meaning / model label
Antibody-mediated rejection: antibodies are immune proteins
T-cell-mediated rejection: T cells are immune cells
Mixed rejection: both rejection processes
No rejection: no recorded rejection
The main question combines all three forms of rejection.

slides.title: Measuring biopsy RNA with NanoString nCounter
paragraphs: RNA includes messages cells make when genes are active. Measuring those messages gives us information about activity in the biopsy tissue.
An assay is a laboratory test. NanoString nCounter is the measurement system used in this study. B-HOT is the panel: the fixed list of RNA molecules selected for measurement.

Probes recognize those selected molecules. Each probe has an identifying molecular barcode, and the instrument counts the barcode signals. The resulting count is a number associated with a named RNA measurement.
For example, IFNG is one of the measurements. Its raw count is four in the public specimen we will follow through the preparation steps and the application.
actions: Explain the instrument and panel, then point to the IFNG count of 4.
visible_cues: RNA includes messages cells make when genes are active.

B-HOT panel: a fixed list of RNA molecules to measure

slides.title: The measurements used by the model
paragraphs: Each specimen has 770 RNA counts. A count corresponds to an assay target, meaning a molecule recognized by one of the probes. There are two roles for those measurements.

The 758 on the left become the model inputs after normalization. Some measure viral RNA, so this is more than a list of human genes. The counts describe the tissue as a whole. A higher signal can reflect more activity within cells, a different mixture of cells, or both.

The other 12 count different housekeeping RNAs. These provide a reference for normalization, which I will show in a moment. After that calculation, we remove those 12 reference measurements. The model receives the 758 normalized values.

slides.title: What the dataset contains
paragraphs: The public data come in two downloads: a metadata file and an archive containing 1,395 individual count files. Our code assembles them into the two tables shown here.

The count table has one row per biopsy specimen and a column for each of the 770 RNA counts. The specimen-information table contains its recorded diagnosis and study group, along with other metadata. The study group identifies which of the authors' two groups contains that specimen.

Specimen ID is unique in each table and matches the rows one to one. GSM6510425 is the same specimen in both. This is how we pair the RNA measurements with the diagnosis used for training and evaluation.
All 1,395 deposited specimens are included. Those are specimen counts. The available records do not establish how many distinct patients they represent.

slides.title: Preparing counts for the model
paragraphs: For each of the 758 counts, we use the same four steps. The right side follows IFNG in our public example, starting with its raw count of four.
Add one and take the base-two logarithm. Adding one allows zero counts, and the logarithm compresses the range. For IFNG, log base two of five is about 2.322.

Next, do that same transformation for each of the 12 housekeeping counts and average them. They measure different RNAs selected to provide a relatively stable reference. Their average helps account for differences in how much measurable RNA a specimen supplies. In this specimen, the reference is about 7.900.

Subtract that reference from each transformed count. For IFNG, 2.322 minus 7.900 gives minus 5.578. So the final value describes the target's signal relative to the reference level. The same raw count can produce a different normalized value in a specimen with a different reference. Those 758 normalized values are the model inputs.
actions: Walk down the four numbered steps, using IFNG for the arithmetic.
visible_cues: For each of the 758 RNA counts / IFNG example
1. Start with the raw count: 4
2. Calculate log2(count + 1): 2.322
3. Average log2(count + 1) for the 12 reference RNAs: 7.900
4. Subtract that reference: 2.322 − 7.900 = −5.578

slides.title: Development and evaluation specimens
paragraphs: The study authors supplied two groups, or cohorts. The discovery cohort has 1,050 specimens, and the validation cohort has 345. Together they contain all 1,395 specimens in the public deposit.

The authors used discovery specimens to develop their classifier and the additional validation group to evaluate it. This project preserves that separation so that model development and the final comparison use different groups.

Within discovery, a saved split assigns 787 specimens to training and 263 to screening, keeping the four diagnosis proportions similar. Training fits the models. Screening compares candidates and chooses the threshold for a rejection flag.

We then evaluate the selected model and threshold on the separate 345 specimens. Each comparison model uses those same evaluation rows. The authors call this group technical validation. The available records do not establish that its patients or centers are entirely separate from discovery.
actions: Follow discovery into training and screening, then move to the separate validation box.
visible_cues: We use the authors' two study groups: discovery and validation cohorts.
Our training / screening split keeps diagnosis proportions similar.

slides.title: Models compared
paragraphs: The constant model gives every specimen the training rejection fraction as its score. This is the baseline: what happens without using any RNA measurements?
The IFNG model uses the one measurement we have already seen. It tests how much information that measurement provides by itself.
Logistic regression combines the measurements using learned weights. Regularization limits the size of those weights, which helps avoid fitting the training examples too closely.
CatBoost combines decision trees. Each tree asks a sequence of questions about measurement values. Together they can represent more complicated relationships than a weighted sum.

All four models use the same specimens, and the RNA models start with the same normalization. We can therefore ask whether combining measurements helps, then whether CatBoost improves enough over logistic regression to justify its added complexity.
actions: Explain each model in table order.
visible_cues: Same RNA preparation and the same evaluation specimens
Constant baseline: one score, the training rejection fraction
IFNG only: a relationship using one RNA measurement
Logistic regression: a weighted combination of 758 measurements; regularization limits weights
CatBoost: a combination of decision trees

slides.title: Choosing a rejection threshold
paragraphs: A threshold turns a model score into a rejection flag. Scores at or above it receive a flag. That gives us two kinds of error to count. A recorded rejection below the threshold is a miss. A recorded no-rejection specimen at or above it is a false flag.

The numbered procedure uses the screening specimens. First, retain thresholds that detect at least 90 percent of recorded rejection specimens. From those thresholds, choose the one that produces the fewest false flags. Keep that model and threshold together for evaluation.
The selected CatBoost threshold is approximately 0.876588. The 90 percent requirement is a choice for this experiment. It is not a clinical requirement or a guarantee on new data.
Also, choosing a threshold does not show that a score is an accurate individual probability. The application therefore calls the output a model score.
actions: Define the two errors, then walk through the screening procedure.
visible_cues: Flag rejection when the model score is at or above the threshold.
Missed rejection: recorded rejection, score below the threshold
False flag: recorded no rejection, score at or above the threshold
Selection using screening specimens
1. Detect at least 90% of recorded rejection cases.
2. Among qualifying choices, minimize false flags.
3. Keep the chosen model and threshold for evaluation.
CatBoost cutoff: 0.876588. The 90% target is an experiment choice.

slides.title: Several measurements reduced false flags
paragraphs: Here are the results on the 345 validation specimens. The two series distinguish the errors: how many of the 169 recorded rejection specimens were missed, and how many of the 176 no-rejection specimens were falsely flagged? The count labels let us compare both errors directly.

The constant model flags every specimen at its selected threshold. It misses zero of 169 rejection specimens, but falsely flags all 176 of 176 no-rejection specimens. That shows why finding every rejection case is not enough to make a useful classifier.
The IFNG-only model misses 14 of 169 rejection specimens and falsely flags 75 of 176 no-rejection specimens. It detects many rejection cases, but it also produces many false flags.

The logistic regression model uses the full panel. It misses 33 of 169 rejection specimens and makes eight false flags among 176 no-rejection specimens. CatBoost misses 25 of 169 and also makes eight false flags among 176.

Compared with IFNG, CatBoost makes 67 fewer false flags but misses 11 more rejection cases. Both parts of that tradeoff matter. The threshold rule used during development results in different error counts in this evaluation group.

Compared with logistic regression, CatBoost detects eight more rejection specimens with the same false-flag count. Combining measurements helps reduce false flags here. The smaller difference between the two full-panel models needs closer examination before we treat it as a dependable advantage.
actions: State both denominators before comparing the bars. Pause on the IFNG tradeoff and the eight-case difference from logistic regression.

slides.title: Most CatBoost misses were T-cell rejection
paragraphs: The original diagnoses help us examine CatBoost's 25 misses. It missed six of 56 antibody-mediated specimens, 18 of 95 T-cell-mediated specimens, and one of 18 mixed specimens.

T-cell rejection accounts for most misses and is also the largest rejection group. About 19 percent of that group was missed, compared with about 11 percent of the antibody-mediated group. One miss among only 18 mixed specimens gives limited evidence about what to expect elsewhere.

Overall, the model detects 144 of 169 rejection specimens, or 85.2 percent. This fraction is called sensitivity. On screening, it detected 157 of 174, or 90.2 percent. The validation result is below the 90 percent requirement we used to choose the threshold.

So the screening rule cannot guarantee performance on new specimens. These errors describe disagreements with the recorded diagnoses. Resolving individual disagreements would require review of the tissue and clinical records.

slides.title: The advantage over logistic regression is uncertain
paragraphs: CatBoost detects eight more of the 169 rejection specimens than logistic regression. Each makes eight false flags among 176 no-rejection specimens. How dependable is that difference?

The first comparison holds the fitted models fixed. We repeatedly resample the validation specimens, allowing a specimen to appear more than once. Both models use the same draws. The 95 percent interval for their difference in detection includes zero, so these results do not establish a clear advantage for CatBoost.

The second comparison asks how the development choice changes with a different split. This follow-up repeats development with 20 saved discovery splits. Each separates fitting, screening, and assessment. The selection rule chooses CatBoost in 13 repetitions and logistic regression in seven.

Those repetitions overlap, so they describe variation with the split. The demonstration retains the selected CatBoost model. Logistic regression remains a credible simpler option to compare in a new cohort.
actions: Explain the fixed-model comparison before the separate development-repeat results.

slides.title: Training and prediction use the same preparation
paragraphs: Training and prediction use the same preparation code. The service reads a CSV, checks the required counts, and normalizes them into 758 model inputs. It then scores those inputs with the saved model.
The command line and the web application both use this code. This matters because a difference in preparation between analysis and the application could change the results.
The response contains specimen ID, model score, threshold, rejection flag, and model version. The version identifies the saved model. The flag records whether the score crossed its threshold.

The service loads the model controlled by this project. The caller supplies the count file. Missing measurements, duplicate names, negative counts, and non-finite values produce an error and stop scoring. The next slide shows both a valid request and a missing-measurement error.

slides.title: Testing the proposed use in ambiguous biopsies
paragraphs: Our current evidence is agreement with recorded diagnoses in one deposited study. The next evaluation needs to test the proposed use in ambiguous biopsies.

First, use new biopsies with patient and center identifiers and documented laboratory quality checks. That would make the study population and the measurement quality clearer. Choose the models and thresholds before examining those results, keeping logistic regression in the comparison.

For the ambiguous cases, compare the usual assessment with assessment that also includes the molecular score. Independent expert review and follow-up outcomes could help judge whether the extra information improves interpretation.

That directly addresses the proposed benefit: does adding molecular evidence help specialists assess difficult biopsies? The classifier and scoring software developed here provide a starting point for that evaluation.
actions: Connect each proposed comparison to the question it would answer.

slides.title: Molecular counts can classify recorded rejection

backups.title: Backup: complete primary comparison
paragraphs: This table compares the four models on the same 345 validation specimens. Miss counts use the 169 recorded rejection specimens. False-flag counts use the 176 recorded no-rejection specimens. Sensitivity is the fraction of rejection specimens flagged. Specificity is the fraction of no-rejection specimens left unflagged.

CatBoost has 85.2 percent sensitivity and 95.5 percent specificity, compared with 80.5 and 95.5 percent for logistic regression. IFNG detects a larger fraction of rejection specimens, at 91.7 percent sensitivity, but its specificity is 57.4 percent. The constant baseline flags everyone.

ROC-AUC describes how well the scores rank rejection above no rejection across possible thresholds. CatBoost has ROC-AUC 0.969, logistic regression 0.956, IFNG 0.842, and the constant baseline 0.500. The error counts describe each model at the threshold selected during development.

backups.title: Backup: normalization and model settings
paragraphs: For each RNA measurement, add one to the raw count and take its base-two logarithm. Subtract the average of the 12 housekeeping counts after applying the same log transformation. This expresses the measurement relative to the specimen's housekeeping reference. The 758 resulting values are the model inputs.

Logistic regression has one additional preparation step. For each normalized measurement, calculate its average and standard deviation across training specimens. Subtract that average and divide by that standard deviation. Reuse those same training values for screening, validation, and future requests. This puts the measurements on comparable scales. CatBoost does not use that additional scaling step here.
Logistic regression uses regularization setting C equal to 0.1. The selected CatBoost model uses 300 trees with depth four and learning rate 0.04. These settings describe the saved comparison.
actions: Use the formula for normalization questions and the training averages for logistic-scaling questions.
visible_cues: Normalized measurement = log2(raw count + 1) minus the mean of 12 housekeeping log2(count + 1) values
Logistic regression: subtract each feature's training mean and divide by its training standard deviation
Reuse those values for later specimens; regularization C = 0.1
CatBoost: no additional feature scaling
300 trees, depth 4, learning rate 0.04

backups.title: Backup: interpreting model scores
paragraphs: This plot groups the 345 validation specimens into ten fixed CatBoost score ranges. Within each range, it compares the average score with the fraction of specimens recorded as rejection. The diagonal shows where the model score and observed fraction would match.

In the highlighted range from 0.8 to 0.9, the mean score is 0.847. Seven of the 16 specimens have recorded rejection, or 43.8 percent. The displayed 95 percent interval for that fraction runs from 23.1 to 66.8 percent. The group is small, and this range was highlighted after inspecting the plot.

A model can rank specimens well while its numerical scores differ from the observed rejection fractions. We did not fit a calibration model on these validation specimens. The application therefore calls its output a model score.

backups.title: Backup: rejection subtype follow-up
paragraphs: This follow-up compared models trained on the four diagnoses with the original model trained on rejection versus no rejection. The table converts each result to the same any-rejection question using rules selected in discovery, so these error counts are comparable.

The original binary CatBoost model misses 25 of 169 rejection specimens with eight false flags among 176 no-rejection specimens. Four-class CatBoost misses 29 with eight false flags. For the separate subtype question, four-class logistic regression correctly identifies ten of 18 mixed diagnoses and makes five false mixed calls among 327 non-mixed specimens.

backups.title: Backup: study, assay and deployment limits
paragraphs: The metadata does not establish that discovery and validation contain independent patients or transplant centers. Uncertainty intervals based on resampling specimens could therefore be too narrow if some specimens are related. Assay groups are also linked to study-group membership, so their effects cannot be cleanly separated.

The software checks required measurements and usable numeric counts. The project did not independently repeat laboratory quality checks such as control-probe or imaging checks. Meaningful inputs still require a compatible assay and completed laboratory quality checks.

The score analysis does not establish reliable individual probabilities, so the service labels its output a model score. We have tested the local research container. Cloud deployment remains deferred.
actions: Answer the relevant limitation and explain what additional evidence would address it.

backups.title: Backup: sources and contributions
paragraphs: Zhang and colleagues supplied the public study and the GSE212160 deposit. This project uses their raw measurements for its own rejection-versus-no-rejection comparison. It does not reconstruct their published classifier.

The project provides saved model runs, shared preparation and prediction software, and a tested local demonstration. Configurations, input hashes, reports, and source code make the quantitative claims inspectable.

The presentation guide draws on Bourne for audience and rehearsal, Kosslyn and colleagues for presentation flaws, Garner and Alley for connecting statements to evidence, and Rougier and colleagues for clear figures. AI assisted with preparing this presentation.

backups.title: Backup: UNOS research connection
paragraphs: UNOS researchers have studied whether artificial intelligence can identify anatomical issues from donor-kidney photographs. They used historical transplant and refusal records to label the images. Their stated aim includes supporting clinical decisions and making anatomical assessment more consistent.

The connection is the research approach: learn from existing assessments to develop an additional source of evidence for transplant professionals. Here, the inputs are RNA measurements and the question concerns rejection in biopsy tissue.
These are different clinical tasks. The UNOS example provides context for the approach. It does not endorse this project or establish that our classifier improves clinical decisions.
